nodes.name: Infinite-horizon discounted MDP
nodes.statement: Consider an infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision process (MDP), defined by the tuple $(\cS, \cA, \cP, r, \rho_0, \gamma)$, where $\cS$ is a finite set of states, $\cA$ is a finite set of actions, $\cP: \cS \times \cA \times \cS \rightarrow \Real$ is the transition probability distribution, $r: \cS \rightarrow \Real$ is the reward function, $\rho_0: \cS \rightarrow \Real$ is the distribution of the initial state $s_0$, and $\gamma \in (0,1)$ is the discount factor.
nodes.section: Preliminaries

nodes.name: Expected discounted reward $\eta(\pi)$
nodes.statement: Let $\pi$ denote a stochastic policy $\pi: \cS \times \cA \rightarrow [0,1]$, and let $\eta(\pi)$ denote its expected discounted reward: \begin{align*} &\eta(\pi) = \Eb{s_0,a_0,\dots}{\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r(s_t)}, \text{ where}\\ &s_0 \sim \rho_0(s_0),\ a_{t} \sim \pi(a_t \given  s_t), \ s_{t+1} \sim P(s_{t+1} \given  s_t, a_t).\nonumber \end{align*}
nodes.section: Preliminaries

nodes.name: State-action value $\Qpi$, value $\Vpi$, advantage $\Api$
nodes.statement: We will use the following standard definitions of the state-action value function $\Qpi$, the value function $\Vpi$, and the advantage function $\Api$: \begin{align*} &\Qpi(s_t, a_t) = \Eb{s_{t+1},a_{t+1},\dots}{\sum_{\delay=0}^{\infty} \gamma^{\delay} r(s_{t+\delay})}, \nonumber\\ &\Vpi(s_t) =\ \Eb{a_t,s_{t+1},\dots}{\sum_{\delay=0}^{\infty} \gamma^{\delay} r(s_{t+\delay})},\\ &A_{\pi}(s,a) =\  Q_{\pi}(s,a) - V_{\pi}(s), \text{ where} \\ &\quad a_{t} \sim \pi(a_t \given  s_t), s_{t+1} \sim P(s_{t+1} \given  s_t, a_t) \text{\ for $t\ge 0$}. \nonumber \end{align*}
nodes.section: Preliminaries

nodes.name: Discounted visitation frequencies $\rho_{\pi}$
nodes.statement: Let $\rho_{\pi}$ be the (unnormalized) discounted visitation frequencies \begin{align} \rho_{\pi}(s) \!=\! P(s_0=s) \!+\! \gamma P(s_1= s) \!+\! \gamma^2 P(s_2 = s) \!+\! \dots, \nonumber \end{align} where $s_0 \sim \rho_0$ and the actions are chosen according to $\pi$.
nodes.section: Preliminaries

nodes.name: Local approximation $L_{\pi}$ (surrogate objective)
nodes.statement: Instead, we introduce the following local approximation to $\eta$: \begin{align} L_{\pi}(\tilpi) = \eta(\pi) + \sum_s \rho_{\pi}(s) \sum_a \tilpi(a \given  s) \Api(s,a). \end{align} Note that $L_{\pi}$ uses the visitation frequency $\rhopi$ rather than $\rho_{\tilpi}$, ignoring changes in state visitation density due to changes in the policy.
nodes.section: Preliminaries

nodes.name: Total variation divergence and $\maxtv$
nodes.statement: The particular distance measure we use is the total variation divergence, which is defined by $\tv{p}{q} = \half \sum_i \abs{p_i - q_i}$ for discrete probability distributions $p,q$. Define $\maxtv(\pi,\tilpi)$ as \begin{align} \maxtv(\pi,\tilpi) = \max_s \tv{\pi(\cdot \given  s)}{\tilpi(\cdot \given  s) }. \end{align}
nodes.section: Monotonic Improvement Guarantee for General Stochastic Policies

nodes.name: $\alpha$-coupled policy pair
nodes.statement: $(\pi,\tilpi)$ is an \textit{$\alpha$-coupled policy pair} if it defines a joint distribution $(a,\tilde{a}) \given s$, such that $P(a \neq \tilde{a} \given s) \le \alpha$ for all $s$. $\pi$ and $\tilpi$ will denote the marginal distributions of $a$ and $\tilde{a}$, respectively.
nodes.section: Appendix: Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Average KL divergence $\meankl{\rho}$
nodes.statement: Instead, we can use a heuristic approximation which considers the average KL divergence: \begin{align*} \meankl{\rho}(\theta_1,\theta_2) \defeq \Eb{s \sim \rho}{\kl{\pi_{\theta_1}(\cdot \given  s)}{\pi_{\theta_2}(\cdot\given s)}}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: Optimization of Parameterized Policies

nodes.name: Expected advantage $\meanadv(s)$
nodes.statement: Define $\meanadv(s)$ to be the expected advantage of $\tilpi$ over $\pi$ at state $s$: \begin{align} \meanadv(s) = \Eb{a \sim \tilpi(\cdot \given s)}{\Api(s, a)}. \end{align}
nodes.section: Appendix: Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Policy improvement bound (Theorem 1)
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha = \maxtv(\piold,\pinew)$. Then the following bound holds: \begin{align} &\eta(\pinew) \ge L_{\piold}(\pinew) - \frac{4 \epsilon \gamma  }{(1-\gamma)^2} \alpha^2 \nonumber\\ &\quad\text{ where } \epsilon = \maxadv \end{align}
nodes.section: Monotonic Improvement Guarantee for General Stochastic Policies

nodes.name: KL-divergence policy improvement bound
nodes.statement: The following bound then follows directly from \Cref{thm:impthm}: \begin{align} &\eta(\tilpi)  \ge L_{\pi}(\tilpi) - C \maxkl(\pi,\tilpi), \nonumber\\ &\qquad \text{ where } C = \frac{4 \epsilon \gamma}{(1-\gamma)^2}. \end{align}
nodes.section: Monotonic Improvement Guarantee for General Stochastic Policies

nodes.name: Monotonic improvement of Algorithm 1
nodes.statement: It follows from \Cref{eq:klminorizer} that \Cref{alg:pialg} is guaranteed to generate a monotonically improving sequence of policies $\eta(\pi_0) \le \eta(\pi_1) \le \eta(\pi_2) \le \dots$.
nodes.section: Monotonic Improvement Guarantee for General Stochastic Policies

nodes.name: Advantage decomposition of policy performance (Lemma 1)
nodes.statement: Given two policies $\pi,\tilpi$, \begin{align} \eta(\tilpi) = \eta(\pi) +  &\Eb{\tau \sim \tilpi}{\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t A_{\pi}(s_t, a_t)} \nonumber \\ \end{align} This expectation is taken over trajectories $\tau \defeq (s_0, a_0, s_1, a_0, \dots)$, and the notation $\Eb{\tau \sim \tilpi}{\dots}$ indicates that actions are sampled from $\tilpi$ to generate $\tau$.
nodes.section: Appendix: Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Coupled expected-advantage bound (Lemma 2)
nodes.statement: Given that $\pi, \tilpi$ are $\alpha$-coupled policies, for all $s$, \begin{align} \abs*{\meanadv(s)} \le 2 \alpha \maxadv \end{align}
nodes.section: Appendix: Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Per-timestep advantage difference bound (Lemma 3)
nodes.statement: Let $(\pi,\tilpi)$ be an $\alpha$-coupled policy pair. Then \begin{align} \abs*{\Eb{s_t \sim \tilpi}{\meanadv(s_t)} - \Eb{s_t \sim \pi}{\meanadv(s_t)}} &\le 2 \alpha \max_s \meanadv(s)\le 4 \alpha (1 - (1 - \alpha)^t)\max_s \abs{\Api(s, a)} \end{align}
nodes.section: Appendix: Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Conservative policy iteration lower bound (Kakade & Langford)
nodes.statement: Kakade and Langford derived the following lower bound: \begin{align} \eta(\pinew) &\!\ge\! L_{\piold}(\pinew) - \frac{2 \epsilon \gamma  }{(1-\gamma)^2} \alpha^2 \nonumber\\ &\text{ where } \epsilon = \max_s \abs*{ \Eb{a \sim \pi'(a\given s)} {\Api(s,a) }}. \end{align}
nodes.section: Preliminaries

nodes.name: Max-KL trust region policy update problem
nodes.statement: \begin{align} &\maximize_{\theta}  L_{\thold}(\theta) \\ &\text{\ \  subject to }  \maxkl(\thold,\theta) \le \delta. \nonumber \end{align}
nodes.section: Optimization of Parameterized Policies

nodes.name: Average-KL trust region policy update problem
nodes.statement: We therefore propose solving the following optimization problem to generate a policy update: \begin{align} &\maximize_{\theta}  L_{\thold}(\theta) \\ &\text{\ \  subject to }  \meankl{\rho_{\thold}}(\thold,\theta) \le \delta. \nonumber \end{align}
nodes.section: Optimization of Parameterized Policies

nodes.name: Sample-based (expectation) trust region problem
nodes.statement: Our optimization problem in \Cref{eq:adv0} is exactly equivalent to the following one, written in terms of expectations: \begin{align} &\maximize_{\theta} \Eb{s \sim \rho_{\thold}, a \sim \isd}{ \frac{\pith(a\given s)}{q(a\given s)} \Qpithold(s,a)}  \\ &\text{\ \  subject to } \Eb{s \sim \rho_{\thold}}{\kl{\pi_{\thold}(\cdot \given  s)}{\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\given s)}} \le \delta.  \nonumber \end{align}
nodes.section: Sample-Based Estimation of the Objective and Constraint

nodes.name: Policy iteration algorithm guaranteeing non-decreasing expected return $\eta$
nodes.statement: \State Initialize $\pi_0$. \For{$i=0,1,2,\dots$ until convergence} \State Compute all advantage values $A_{\pi_i}(s,a)$. \State Solve the constrained optimization problem \begin{align*} \qquad\pi_{i+1} &=\argmax_{\pi} \lrbrack{ L_{\pi_i}(\pi) - C \maxkl(\pi_i,\pi) } \nonumber \\ &\!\!\!\!\!\text{ where $C=4\epsilon\gamma/(1-\gamma)^2$}\\ &\!\!\!\!\!\text{ and } L_{\pi_i}(\pi) \!=\! \eta(\pi_i) \!+\! \sum_s \rho_{\pi_i}\!(s)\! \sum_a \! \pi(a \given  s) A_{\pi_i}(s,a) \nonumber \end{align*} \EndFor
nodes.section: Monotonic Improvement Guarantee for General Stochastic Policies

nodes.name: Practical TRPO policy optimization algorithm
nodes.statement: The algorithms repeatedly perform the following steps: \begin{enumerate} \item Use the \singlepath{} or \vine{} procedures to collect a set of state-action pairs along with Monte Carlo estimates of their $Q$-values. \item By averaging over samples, construct the estimated objective and constraint in \Cref{eq:trprobexp}. \item Approximately solve this constrained optimization problem to update the policy's parameter vector $\theta$. We use the conjugate gradient algorithm followed by a line search, which is altogether only slightly more expensive than computing the gradient itself. See \Cref{sec:cg} for details. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: Practical Algorithm

nodes.name: Minorization-maximization (MM) interpretation
nodes.statement: This algorithm is a type of minorization-maximization (MM) algorithm \cite{hunter2004tutorial}, which is a class of methods that also includes expectation maximization. In the terminology of MM algorithms, $M_i$ is the surrogate function that minorizes $\eta$ with equality at $\pi_i$. This algorithm is also reminiscent of proximal gradient methods and mirror descent.
nodes.section: Monotonic Improvement Guarantee for General Stochastic Policies

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: First note that $A_{\pi}(s,a) = \Eb{s' \sim P(s' \given s,a)}{r(s) + \gamma \Vpi(s') - \Vpi(s)}$. Therefore, \begin{align} &\Eb{\tau \given \tilpi}{\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t A_{\pi}(s_t, a_t)}\\ &= \Eb{\tau \given \tilpi}{\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t (r(s_t) + \gamma \Vpi(s_{t+1}) - \Vpi(s_t))}\\ &= \Eb{\tau \given \tilpi}{-\Vpi(s_0)+ \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r(s_t)}  \\ &= -\Eb{s_0}{\Vpi(s_0)}+\Eb{\tau \given \tilpi}{\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t r(s_t)}  \\ &=  -\eta(\pi) + \eta(\tilpi) \end{align} Rearranging, the result follows.
nodes.section: Appendix: Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \meanadv(s) &= \Eb{\tilde{a} \sim \tilpi}{\Api(s,\tilde{a})} =\Eb{(a,\tilde{a}) \sim (\pi,\tilpi)}{\Api(s,\tilde{a}) - \Api(s, a)} \quad\text{since \quad$\Eb{a \sim \pi}{\Api(s,a)}=0$}\\ &= P(a \neq \tilde{a} \given s) \Eb{(a,\tilde{a}) \sim (\pi,\tilpi) \given a \neq \tilde{a}}{\Api(s,\tilde{a}) - \Api(s, a)}\\ \abs{\meanadv(s)} &\le \alpha \cdot 2 \maxadv \end{align}

Namely, we have pairs of trajectories $	au, 	ilde{	au}$, where $	au$ is obtained by taking actions from $\pi$, and $	ilde{	au}$ is obtained by taking actions from $	ilpi$, where the same random seed is used to generate both trajectories. We will consider the advantage of $	ilpi$ over $\pi$ at timestep $t$, and decompose this expectation based on whether $\pi$ agrees with $	ilpi$ at all timesteps $i<t$. Let $n_t$ denote the number of times that $a_i

t = 0}{\meanadv(\st)} + P(n_t > 0) \Eb{\st \sim \pi |

Subtracting \Cref{decomp-pitil,decomp-pi}, we get  egin{align} \Eb{\st \sim 	ilpi}{\meanadv(s_t)} - \Eb{\st \sim \pi}{\meanadv(s_t)} &= P(n_t > 0) \lrparena*{ \Eb{\st \sim 	ilpi | 
t > 0}{\meanadv(s_t)} - \Eb{\st \sim \pi |

t > 0}{\meanadv(s_t)} - \Eb{\st \sim \pi |

Plugging \Cref{nineq} and \Cref{epsineq} into \Cref{diff-ineq}, we get  egin{align} \abs*{\Eb{\st \sim 	ilpi}{\meanadv(s_t)} - \Eb{\st \sim \pi}{\meanadv(s_t)}} \le 4 \alpha (1 - (1 - \alpha)^t) \maxadv \end{align}

nodes.name: Coupling proof of Theorem 1 (assembly)
nodes.statement: The preceding Lemma bounds the difference in expected advantage at each timestep $t$. We can sum over time to bound the difference between $\eta(\tilpi)$ and $L_{\pi}(\tilpi)$. Subtracting \Cref{etadef} and \Cref{tilpidef}, and defining $\epsilon=\maxadv$, \begin{align} \abs*{\eta(\tilpi) - L_{\pi}(\tilpi)} &=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t \abs*{ \Eb{\tau \sim \tilpi}{\meanadv(s_t)}-\Eb{\tau \sim \pi}{\meanadv(s_t)} }\\ &\le \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t \cdot 4\epsilon \alpha (1 - (1 - \alpha)^t)\\ &= 4\epsilon \alpha \lrparen{\frac{1}{1 - \gamma} - \frac{1}{1 - \gamma(1- \alpha)}}\\ &= \frac{4\alpha^2 \gamma \epsilon}{(1 - \gamma)(1 - \gamma(1- \alpha ))}\\ &\le \frac{4\alpha^2 \gamma \epsilon}{(1 - \gamma)^2} \end{align} Last, to replace $\alpha$ by the total variation divergence, we need to use the correspondence between TV divergence and coupled random variables: \begin{quote} Suppose $p_X$ and $p_Y$ are distributions with $\tv{p_X}{p_Y} = \alpha$. Then there exists a joint distribution $(X,Y)$ whose marginals are $p_X, p_Y$, for which $X = Y$ with probability $1-\alpha$. \end{quote} See \cite{levin2009markov}, Proposition 4.7. It follows that if we have two policies $\pi$ and $\tilpi$ such that $\max_s \tv{\pi(\cdot \given  s)}{\tilpi(\cdot \given  s) } \le \alpha$, then we can define an $\alpha$-coupled policy pair $(\pi,\tilpi)$ with appropriate marginals. Taking $\alpha=\max_s \tv{\pi(\cdot \given  s)}{\tilpi(\cdot \given  s) } \le \alpha$ in \Cref{fracsineq}, \Cref{thm:impthm} follows.

nodes.name: Proof of monotonic improvement of Algorithm 1
nodes.statement: To see this, let $M_i(\pi) = L_{\pi_i}(\pi) - C \maxkl(\pi_i, \pi)$. Then \begin{align} &\eta(\pi_{i+1}) \ge  M_i(\pi_{i+1}) \text{ by Equation~\eqref{eq:klminorizer}} \nonumber \\ &\eta(\pi_{i}) =  M_i(\pi_i), \text{ therefore,} \nonumber \\ &\eta(\pi_{i+1}) - \eta(\pi_i) \ge M_i(\pi_{i+1}) - M(\pi_i). \end{align} Thus, by maximizing $M_i$ at each iteration, we guarantee that the true objective $\eta$ is non-decreasing.

nodes.name: Set up trajectory coupling and disagreement count $n_t$
nodes.statement: Given the coupled policy pair $(\pi, \tilpi)$, we can also obtain a coupling over the trajectory distributions produced by $\pi$ and $\tilpi$, respectively. Namely, we have pairs of trajectories $\tau, \tilde{\tau}$, where $\tau$ is obtained by taking actions from $\pi$, and $\tilde{\tau}$ is obtained by taking actions from $\tilpi$, where the same random seed is used to generate both trajectories. We will consider the advantage of $\tilpi$ over $\pi$ at timestep $t$, and decompose this expectation based on whether $\pi$ agrees with $\tilpi$ at all timesteps $i<t$. Let $n_t$ denote the number of times that $a_i \neq \tilde{a}_i$ for $i < t$, i.e., the number of times that $\pi$ and $\tilpi$ disagree before timestep $t$.

nodes.name: Decompose expectations by $n_t$; equal $n_t=0$ terms
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \Eb{s_t \sim \tilpi}{\meanadv(s_t)} = P(n_t=0)\Eb{s_t \sim \tilpi \given n_t = 0}{\meanadv(s_t)} + P(n_t>0)\Eb{s_t \sim \tilpi \given n_t > 0}{\meanadv(s_t)} \end{align} The expectation decomposes similarly for actions are sampled using $\pi$: \begin{align} \Eb{\st \sim \pi}{\meanadv(\st)} = P(n_t = 0) \Eb{\st \sim \pi | \nt = 0}{\meanadv(\st)} + P(n_t > 0) \Eb{\st \sim \pi | \nt > 0}{\meanadv(\st)} \end{align} Note that the $n_t=0$ terms are equal: \begin{align} \Eb{s_t \sim {\color{red} \tilpi} \given n_t = 0}{\meanadv(s_t)}=\Eb{s_t \sim {\color{red} \pi} \given n_t = 0}{\meanadv(s_t)}, \end{align} because $n_t=0$ indicates that $\pi$ and $\tilpi$ agreed on all timesteps less than $t$.
nodes.section: Appendix: Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Subtract the two decompositions
nodes.statement: Subtracting \Cref{decomp-pitil,decomp-pi}, we get \begin{align} \Eb{\st \sim \tilpi}{\meanadv(s_t)} - \Eb{\st \sim \pi}{\meanadv(s_t)} &= P(n_t > 0) \lrparena*{ \Eb{\st \sim \tilpi | \nt > 0}{\meanadv(s_t)} - \Eb{\st \sim \pi | \nt > 0}{\meanadv(s_t)} } \end{align}
nodes.section: Appendix: Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Bound $P(n_t>0) \le 1-(1-\alpha)^t$
nodes.statement: By definition of $\alpha$, $P(\pi,\tilpi \text{ agree at timestep $i$}) \ge 1-\alpha$, so $P(n_t = 0) \ge (1-\alpha)^t$, and \begin{align} P(n_t > 0) \le 1 - (1 - \alpha)^t \end{align}
nodes.section: Appendix: Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Bound the conditional expected-advantage difference
nodes.statement:
Next, note that  egin{align} \abs*{\Eb{\st \sim 	ilpi | 
t > 0}{\meanadv(s_t)} - \Eb{\st \sim \pi | 
t > 0}{\meanadv(s_t)}} &\le \abs*{\Eb{\st \sim 	ilpi | 
t > 0}{\meanadv(s_t)}} +\abs*{\Eb{\st \sim \pi | 
t > 0}{\meanadv(s_t)}}\ &\le 4\alpha \maxadv \end{align} Where the second inequality follows from \Cref{advbound}.

nodes.name: Plug bounds together to conclude
nodes.statement: Plugging \Cref{nineq} and \Cref{epsineq} into \Cref{diff-ineq}, we get \begin{align} \abs*{\Eb{\st \sim \tilpi}{\meanadv(s_t)} - \Eb{\st \sim \pi}{\meanadv(s_t)}} \le 4 \alpha (1 - (1 - \alpha)^t) \maxadv \end{align}

nodes.name: Sum per-timestep bound over time
nodes.statement: The preceding Lemma bounds the difference in expected advantage at each timestep $t$. We can sum over time to bound the difference between $\eta(\tilpi)$ and $L_{\pi}(\tilpi)$. Subtracting \Cref{etadef} and \Cref{tilpidef}, and defining $\epsilon=\maxadv$, \begin{align} \abs*{\eta(\tilpi) - L_{\pi}(\tilpi)} &=\sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t \abs*{ \Eb{\tau \sim \tilpi}{\meanadv(s_t)}-\Eb{\tau \sim \pi}{\meanadv(s_t)} }\\ &\le \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \gamma^t \cdot 4\epsilon \alpha (1 - (1 - \alpha)^t)\\ &= 4\epsilon \alpha \lrparen{\frac{1}{1 - \gamma} - \frac{1}{1 - \gamma(1- \alpha)}}\\ &= \frac{4\alpha^2 \gamma \epsilon}{(1 - \gamma)(1 - \gamma(1- \alpha ))}\\ &\le \frac{4\alpha^2 \gamma \epsilon}{(1 - \gamma)^2} \end{align}

nodes.name: Invoke TV-divergence / coupling correspondence
nodes.statement: Last, to replace $\alpha$ by the total variation divergence, we need to use the correspondence between TV divergence and coupled random variables: \begin{quote} Suppose $p_X$ and $p_Y$ are distributions with $\tv{p_X}{p_Y} = \alpha$. Then there exists a joint distribution $(X,Y)$ whose marginals are $p_X, p_Y$, for which $X = Y$ with probability $1-\alpha$. \end{quote} See \cite{levin2009markov}, Proposition 4.7.

nodes.name: Conclude Theorem 1
nodes.statement: It follows that if we have two policies $\pi$ and $\tilpi$ such that $\max_s \tv{\pi(\cdot \given  s)}{\tilpi(\cdot \given  s) } \le \alpha$, then we can define an $\alpha$-coupled policy pair $(\pi,\tilpi)$ with appropriate marginals. Taking $\alpha=\max_s \tv{\pi(\cdot \given  s)}{\tilpi(\cdot \given  s) } \le \alpha$ in \Cref{fracsineq}, \Cref{thm:impthm} follows.

nodes.name: Set up resolvents $G,\tilG$ and target
nodes.statement: Let $G = (1 + \gamma \Ppi + (\gamma \Ppi)^2 + \dots) = (1-\gamma \Ppi)^{-1}$, and similarly Let $\tilG = (1 + \gamma \Ppitil + (\gamma \Ppitil)^2 + \dots) = (1-\gamma \Ppitil)^{-1}$. We will use the convention that $\rho$ (a density on state space) is a vector and $r$ (a reward function on state space) is a dual vector (i.e., linear functional on vectors), thus $r \rho$ is a scalar meaning the expected reward under density $\rho$. Note that $\eta(\pi) = rG\rho_0$, and $\eta(\tilpi) = c \tilG \rho_0$. Let $\dP = \Ppitil - \Ppi$. We want to bound $\eta(\tilpi) - \eta(\pi) = r(\tilG - G)\rho_0$.
nodes.section: Appendix: Perturbation Theory Proof of Policy Improvement Bound

nodes.name: Standard perturbation-theory expansion
nodes.statement: We start with some standard perturbation theory manipulations. \begin{align} G^{-1} - \tilG^{-1} &= (1-\gamma \Ppi) - (1-\gamma \Ppitil) \nonumber \\ &= \gamma \dP. \end{align} Left multiply by $G$ and right multiply by $\tilG$. \begin{align} \tilG - G &= \gamma G \dP\tilG \nonumber \\ \tilG &= G + \gamma G \dP\tilG \end{align} Substituting the right-hand side into $\tilG$ gives \begin{align} \tilG   &= G + \gamma G \dP G + \gamma^2 G \dP G \dP \tilG \end{align} So we have \begin{align} \eta(\tilpi) - \eta(\pi) = r(\tilG - G)\rho = \gamma r G \dP G \rho_0 + \gamma^2 r G \dP G \dP \tilG \rho_0 \end{align}

nodes.name: Approximately solve to update parameters
nodes.statement: Approximately solve this constrained optimization problem to update the policy's parameter vector $\theta$. We use the conjugate gradient algorithm followed by a line search, which is altogether only slightly more expensive than computing the gradient itself. See \Cref{sec:cg} for details.
